issues.legal_issue: A tenant-at-will’s actual possession of agricultural land is not the intermediary landlord’s khas possession merely because the landlord has a right to recover possession.
material_facts: The defendants were tenants-at-will cultivating agricultural land in their own account and were in actual possession when the estate vested in the State.
A notice to quit had been served, but the tenancy would not end until the end of the agricultural year, so the tenants could remain in possession at vesting.
The intermediary landlord had, at most, a right to recover possession after the tenancy was properly terminated; the landlord was not himself cultivating the land through the tenants.
The eviction suit was brought after the estate had vested.
issues.conclusion: The land was not in the intermediary’s khas possession on the date of vesting. The intermediary’s right to recover possession did not amount to khas possession, and after vesting the intermediary could not maintain the suit for eviction.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(k), 3, 4 and 6(1) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, khas possession requires actual possession through the intermediary’s own cultivation, servants, hired labour or hired stock; a bare right to possess is insufficient. Section 6(1)(b) concerns land held in the direct possession of a temporary lessee of an estate or tenure and does not apply merely because a tenant-at-will occupies the land. The Court relied on Surajnath Ahir v. Prithinath Singh, Ram Ran Bijai Singh v. Behari Singh, and Gurucharan Singh v. Kamla Singh, and held that interpretation of the agrarian-reform scheme should favour the actual cultivator.

rule.if: agricultural_land_recovery_proceeding_after_vesting and tenant_at_will_in_actual_possession_on_vesting and tenant_cultivates_on_own_account and termination_notice_not_yet_expired and landlord_has_only_right_to_recover_possession

predicates.agricultural_land_recovery_proceeding_af: An intermediary seeks recovery of agricultural land after the estate containing it has vested in the State.
predicates.tenant_at_will_in_actual_possession_on_v: A tenant-at-will is physically occupying the land when the estate vests.
predicates.tenant_cultivates_on_own_account: The tenant carries out cultivation on the tenant’s own account rather than as the landlord’s servant or hired labourer.
predicates.termination_notice_not_yet_expired: A notice to terminate the tenancy has been given but has not yet taken effect.
predicates.landlord_has_only_right_to_recover_posse: The landlord has a right to seek possession but has not obtained actual possession of the land.

issues.definition: When an intermediary seeks agricultural land after vesting and a tenant-at-will remains in actual possession cultivating independently under a tenancy not yet terminated, the intermediary’s right to recover possession does not establish actual possession and the intermediary cannot sue after vesting.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant-at-will of agricultural land cannot be evicted until the tenancy is terminated by proper notice expiring with the agricultural year.
material_facts: The tenants-at-will occupied agricultural land and held from year to year.
In earlier litigation between the parties, the High Court had determined that the tenants could not be evicted without notice to quit ending with the agricultural year.
The notice served in the later eviction proceedings was to expire at the end of the agricultural year.
issues.conclusion: The Court affirmed that an agricultural tenant-at-will must receive notice terminating the tenancy, and that the notice must expire with the end of the agricultural year.
issues.legal_principle: A tenant-at-will is still a tenant and may hold possession against the landlord until the tenancy is terminated according to law. For agricultural land, the notice must expire with the agricultural year. The Court agreed with the earlier High Court decision between the parties, relied on the discussion in Halsbury’s Laws of England, and declined to follow Sudhir Kumar Majumdar v. Dhirendra Nath Biswas, which had treated formal notice as unnecessary. Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was discussed but was not necessary to the holding.

predicates.agricultural_tenant_at_will: A person occupies agricultural land as a tenant-at-will.
predicates.landlord_seeks_eviction: The landlord seeks to remove the tenant from the land.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks to evict an agricultural tenant-at-will, eviction requires notice that terminates the tenancy at the end of the agricultural year.

issues.legal_issue: Additional evidence of a State settlement obtained on the basis of a decree under appeal may be refused where its admission would disadvantage the opposing party and the settlement’s validity cannot be determined in the suit.
material_facts: The appellant sought permission to introduce additional evidence of a settlement of the land with the intermediary by the State.
The asserted settlement had been obtained on the basis of a trial-court or first-appellate-court decree that became interlocutory during further appeals.
Admitting the evidence at that stage might disadvantage the respondents, and the validity of the asserted settlement could not be determined in the suit.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld rejection of the application to adduce additional evidence and held that the appellant could not rely in this suit on a settlement obtained on the basis of a decree that had become interlocutory.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Order 41, Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure and held that the proposed evidence could properly be refused where its admission would put the opposing party at a disadvantage and the validity of the asserted settlement was not an issue that could be determined in the suit. A party cannot take advantage in the proceeding of a settlement obtained on the basis of a decree that became interlocutory through appeal.

rule.if: appellate_application_to_add_evidence and settlement_claimed_under_nonfinal_decree and admission_would_disadvantage_opponent and settlement_validity_cannot_be_determined_in_suit

predicates.appellate_application_to_add_evidence: A party in an appellate proceeding asks to introduce additional evidence.
predicates.settlement_claimed_under_nonfinal_decree: The proposed evidence concerns a settlement obtained on the basis of a decree that became interlocutory during appeal.
predicates.admission_would_disadvantage_opponent: Admitting the evidence at that stage would put the opposing party at a disadvantage.
predicates.settlement_validity_cannot_be_determined: The validity of the asserted settlement cannot be resolved in the suit in which the evidence is offered.

issues.definition: An appellate court may reject an application to add evidence of a settlement based on a nonfinal decree when admitting it would disadvantage the opponent and the suit cannot determine the settlement’s validity.

issues.legal_issue: A contention available to a party but abandoned in the High Court cannot be raised again before the Supreme Court.
material_facts: The appellant argued before the Supreme Court that the respondents’ appeal in the High Court should have been dismissed for failure to comply with an order concerning service of notice.
The contention was available to the appellant in the High Court but was not raised there.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the contention had been abandoned and could not be re-agitated before it.
issues.legal_principle: A party cannot raise before the Supreme Court a contention that was available but abandoned in the High Court. The Court relied on Jayarama Reddy v. Revenue Divisional Officer and Land Acquisition Officer, Kurnool.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: A party seeks relief in an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.contention_available_in_high_court: The party could have raised the contention in the High Court.
predicates.contention_not_raised_there: The party did not raise the contention in the High Court.

issues.definition: In a Supreme Court appeal, a contention available but not raised in the High Court cannot be raised again.

issues.legal_issue: A court retains the power to extend a time limit it has fixed for taking a procedural step.
material_facts: The High Court fixed a time for taking steps to serve notice in an appeal and initially directed that the appeal would stand dismissed if the steps were not taken.
The High Court subsequently extended the time for taking the steps.
The appellant argued that the appeal had already stood dismissed under the initial order.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the High Court retained power to extend the time it had fixed, so the appeal had not stood dismissed under the initial order.
issues.legal_principle: When a court fixes time for doing a procedural act, it retains the power to extend that time. The Court applied that principle to the successive procedural orders in the High Court appeal.

predicates.appellate_proceeding_with_court_fixed_co: An appellate court has fixed a time for a party to complete a procedural step.

issues.definition: When an appellate court fixes time for a procedural step, it retains the power to extend that time.
